# Examining the Relationships Among Teacher Characteristics, Collaboration, AI- Integrated TPACK, and Teacher Enthusiasm: A Multi- Group Analysis by Gender

Deniz Kaya[1 ](#examining-the-relationships-among-teacher-characteristics-collaboration-ai--integrated-tpack-and-teacher-enthusiasm-a-multi--group-analysis-by-gender)\| Ömer Faruk Ursavaş[2 ](#examining-the-relationships-among-teacher-characteristics-collaboration-ai--integrated-tpack-and-teacher-enthusiasm-a-multi--group-analysis-by-gender)\| Hatice Yildiz Durak[3](mailto:)

1Mathematics Education Program, Department of Mathematics and Science Education, Faculty of Education, Nevşehir Haci Bektaş Veli University, Nevşehir, Turkey \| 2Department of Computer Sciences, Faculty of Science, Karadeniz Technic University, Trabzon, Turkey \| 3Department of Educational Science, Instructional Technology, Eregli Faculty of Education, Necmettin Erbakan University, Konya, Turkey

**Correspondence:** Hatice Yildiz Durak ([hatyil05@gmail.com;](mailto:hatyil05@gmail.com) [hatice.yildizdurak@erbakan.edu.tr)](mailto:hatice.yildizdurak@erbakan.edu.tr) **Received:** 16 April 2025 \| **Revised:** 19 June 2025 \| **Accepted:** 11 July 2025

**Funding:** The authors received no specific funding for this work. **Keywords:** AI \| AI- TPACK \| collaboration \| enthusiasm \| gender \| multi- group analysis \| structural equation modelling

## ABSTRACT The aim of this study was to examine the relationships among teacher characteristics, collaboration, the level of artificial intelligence- integrated technological pedagogical content knowledge (AI- TPACK), and teacher enthusiasm, and to compara- tively evaluate these relationships through multi- group analysis (MGA) based on gender. The research model was tested using Partial Least Squares–Structural Equation Modelling (PLS- SEM) to analyse the structural relationships among the variables. Data were collected from 323 teachers working at various school levels across the seven geographical regions of Türkiye, repre- senting diversity in terms of educational background, professional experience, and subject area. In addition to the Demographic Information Form, the AI- TPACK Scale, Teacher Enthusiasm Scale, and Teacher Collaboration Scale were used during the data collection process. The findings of the study reveal that teacher collaboration has significant and positive effects on both TPACK and AI- TPACK components. However, age, educational level, professional experience, and school type did not significantly predict teacher collaboration. Pedagogical knowledge (PK), pedagogical content knowledge (PCK), and AI- based technological knowledge (AI- TK) had significant effects on teacher enthusiasm, whereas content knowledge (CK), AI- based technological con- tent knowledge (AI- TCK), AI- based technological pedagogical knowledge (AI- TPK), and AI- TPACK did not show any significant effect. Contextual variables such as ICT usage competence, AI usage experience, and AI usage intensity did not have a significant effect on teacher enthusiasm. Gender- based analysis results revealed that the effects of teacher collaboration on PK, CK, PCK, and AI- TPACK components differed significantly between male and female teachers, whereas the effects on AI- TCK and AI- TPK components were significant only among female teachers. It was found that PK significantly predicted teacher enthusiasm only among female teachers, while AI- TK significantly predicted teacher enthusiasm only among male teachers.

AI- Ed is leading profound structural transforma- tions in key areas such as the design of next- generation digital learning environments responsive to students' individual needs and learning styles (Sun et al. 2022), the support of instructional decision- making through big data analytics (Mishra et al. 2023), and the restructuring of instructional strategies in accordance with the principles of flexibility, validity, and adaptability (Stolpe and Hallström 2024).

The positioning of digital technologies as a transformative driv- ing force in education has led to intensified theoretical discus- sions about how these technologies should be designed within instructional contexts, which learning outcomes they should be associated with, and how they should be integrated into peda- gogical processes. In this context, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework developed by Mishra and Koehler (2006) provides a theoretical foundation for the ef- fective integration of technology in education and is widely rec- ognised in the literature as one of the most accepted models in this domain. However, the growing impact of AI technologies in education has brought the restructuring of the TPACK model to the forefront. Accordingly, researchers have introduced the concept of AI- TPACK, which incorporates the perspective of AI into the technology dimension and redefines instructional com- petencies accordingly (Celik [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Lan et al. 2025; Lorenz and Romeike 2023; Mishra et al. 2023; Ning et al. 2024).

TPACK defines the types of knowledge that teachers need to effectively and meaningfully design instruction by integrat- ing technology with content and didactic knowledge (Koehler et al. 2017; Yildiz Durak 2021). This framework is based on three core domains of knowledge: content knowledge (CK), pedagog- ical knowledge (PK), and technological knowledge (TK). The intersections of these components—pedagogical content knowl- edge (PCK), technological content knowledge (TCK), and tech- nological pedagogical knowledge (TPK)—reflect the teacher's ability to integrate content, pedagogical strategies, and technol- ogy. TPACK represents a holistic synthesis of these three do- mains and reflects the teacher's competence to use technology in ways that are contextually appropriate, pedagogically meaning- ful, and instructionally effective. On the other hand, AI- TPACK defines the domains of knowledge required for teachers to effec- tively integrate AI technologies into their teaching. AI- TK refers to the ability to recognise and use AI tools; AI- TPK refers to un- derstanding their pedagogical impact; AI- TCK involves linking AI with subject content; AI- TPACK represents the integration of all these domains for effective instruction; and AI- Ethics re- fers to the competence to ensure the fair and responsible use of AI in education (Celik [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Lorenz and Romeike 2023; Mishra et al. 2023; Ning et al. 2024).

Theoretical developments shaped within the AI- TPACK frame- work raise fundamental questions about how teachers perceive AI technologies, to what extent they integrate these technolo- gies into their professional practices, and which individual or contextual variables play a determining role in this process. In particular, complex structures such as the relationship between teachers' individual and professional characteristics and their level of collaboration, the impact of collaboration on AI- TPACK components, and the interaction between these components and teacher enthusiasm have not yet been adequately examined in 

2 of 27

the existing literature using a systematic and holistic approach. Furthermore, the scarcity of empirical studies that reveal how these relationships differ based on gender also highlights a sig- nificant gap in the field.

To address this gap, the present study places specific emphasis on four core variables that are theoretically and practically linked to AI- Ed pedagogical practice: teacher characteristics, professional collaboration, teacher enthusiasm, and gender. Teacher charac- teristics—such as age, education level, experience, and school context—are conceptualised as background factors that may shape collaboration and pedagogical orientations. Teacher col- laboration is approached as a mediating process through which professional knowledge and practices are co- constructed and AI- related competencies are developed. Teacher enthusiasm, in turn, is considered a central affective outcome that reflects moti- vational engagement and professional vitality in technology- rich teaching environments. Finally, gender is included as a moder- ator variable to explore how the interplay between these factors may differ across demographic lines. By positioning these vari- ables within an integrated structural model, the study aims to move beyond purely technological explanations and offer a more holistic account of the cognitive, social, and emotional dynamics surrounding AI- TPACK in education.

This study aims to address the gaps in question by analysing the relationship between teachers' individual and professional char- acteristics and their collaboration, the effect of this collaboration on AI- TPACK components, and the predictive role of these com- ponents on teacher enthusiasm. In addition, the study aims to take a holistic approach to AI- Ed by evaluating the contribution of situational variables—such as AI usage experience, AI usage intensity, and information and communication technology (ICT) competence—to teacher enthusiasm. In this regard, the study seeks to answer the following research questions (RQs):

RQ1. _To what extent do teachers' background characteristics in-_ _fluence their collaboration_?

RQ2. _To what extent does teacher collaboration predict AI- TPACK components_?

RQ3. _Do the AI- TPACK components significantly affect teacher enthusiasm_?

RQ4. _To what extent do contextual variables (ICT usage compe-_ _tence, AI usage experience, and AI usage intensity) predict teacher enthusiasm_?

**1.1 \| Related Research**

The integration of AI in education, particularly when evalu- ated within the theoretical framework of TPACK, emerges as a multidimensional and continuously evolving phenomenon situated at the intersection of pedagogical, technological, and content- related components. Studies in the literature reveal that the AI- TPACK framework offers an innovative struc- ture that enables not only technological integration but also pedagogical transformation within teaching and learning processes. In this context, the potential of the framework to 

_European Journal of Education,_ 2025

enrich personalised learning experiences and to make instruc- tional design more effective and flexible has been frequently emphasised. For instance, in the study conducted by Karataş and Ataç (2024), the traditional TPACK and AI–TPACK com- petencies of 304 preservice English teachers were examined in detail using structural equation modelling (SEM). The find- ings indicated that while the teacher candidates demonstrated high levels of TK and AI- TK, they had lower competencies in integrating this knowledge with pedagogical CK. Gender- based analyses revealed that male teacher candidates scored significantly higher than their female counterparts across all dimensions of AI- TPACK—particularly in AI- TK and AI- TCK. In the study conducted by Feldman- Maggor et al. (2025), the integration of AI- based generative (GenAI) tools into chemis- try education was examined through the lens of the TPACK framework. It was emphasised that for teachers to use GenAI tools effectively, they need not only TK, but also PK and AI literacy. The analyses conducted through three case studies demonstrated that GenAI- specific situations could not be suf- ficiently explained within the TPACK framework.

In a study conducted by Runge et al. (2025) with 143 participants, those who attended AI- focused courses were found to have higher levels of AI- TPACK and perceived usefulness of AI. No significant difference was observed between participation and perceived ease of use. AI- TPACK levels were found to be posi- tively associated with perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. However, no significant relationship was found between AI- TPACK and behavioural intention or actual use. While per- ceived usefulness was significantly associated with behavioural intention, no significant relationship was observed between per- ceived ease of use and behavioural intention. In contrast, both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use were found to be significantly associated with actual use. In a study conducted by Al- Abdullatif ([2024)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) with 237 faculty members, the acceptance of GenAI technologies was examined in relation to AI literacy, intelligent TPACK, perceived trust, perceived ease of use, and perceived usefulness. AI literacy was found to be directly asso- ciated with perceived ease of use and the acceptance of GenAI technologies. AI literacy also had a direct effect on intelligent TPACK and perceived trust. While the direct effect of intelligent TPACK on acceptance was not found to be significant, an in- direct effect was identified through perceived ease of use. On the other hand, the effect of AI literacy on perceived useful- ness and ease of use was mediated indirectly through perceived trust and intelligent TPACK. In a study conducted by Hava and Babayiğit  (2025) with 401 teachers, the relationship between AI- TPACK and digital competence levels was examined. In the study, teachers' AI- TPACK levels were found to be below aver- age, whereas their digital competence levels were above average. Among the AI- TPACK subdimensions, the area in which teach- ers showed the lowest level of competence was the integrated AI- TPACK component that combines all knowledge domains. In contrast, the highest levels of competence were observed in the AI- TCK and AI- TPK dimensions. Significant and positive rela- tionships were identified between teachers' digital competence levels and their AI- TPACK competencies.

In the study conducted by Cheng and Xie (2018), the relation- ships among teachers' characteristics, TPACK levels, and value beliefs were examined in both intervention and non- intervention 

contexts. The findings indicate that teachers' value beliefs re- garding technology were significant and strong predictors of the technology- related knowledge domains, namely TK, TCK, TPK, and TPCK. In the non- intervention setting, male teachers were found to have higher levels of TK, TCK, and TPK compared to female teachers. Additionally, TK levels were observed to de- crease as age and experience increased. Technology use had a positive impact on the technology- based components of TPACK. Moreover, value beliefs played a moderating role in the rela- tionships between age, gender, technology use, and TPACK. In another study conducted by Koh et al. (2014), the constructivist- oriented TPACK (C- TPACK) perceptions of 354 teachers were examined. The study analysed the relationships between teach- ers' C- TPACK levels and the TPACK components (C- TK, C- PK, CK, C- PCK, C- TPK, TCK) as well as demographic variables such as age, gender, teaching experience, and teaching level. The findings revealed that teachers had lower levels of confidence, particularly in the constructivist technology- related knowledge domains, namely C- TK, C- TPK, and TCK. Regression analysis results showed that C- TPK, C- TK, and TCK were the strongest predictors of C- TPACK. While age and gender had no significant effect, teaching level and teaching experience had a limited in- fluence on perceptions of C- TPACK.

Although the existing literature has made significant prog- ress in understanding the development of AI- TPACK, many fundamental questions regarding the role of individual and contextual factors in shaping affective outcomes—such as teacher collaboration and teacher enthusiasm—remain un- answered. This study aimed to examine the effect of teacher characteristics—such as age, experience, educational level, and school type—on professional collaboration, investigat- ing how these individual variables shape teachers' tendencies toward collaboration. This assumption is supported by previ- ous studies showing that such demographic and professional variables shape teachers' orientations regarding knowledge sharing, trust in colleagues, pedagogical behaviours affecting the quality of learning processes, teaching tenure, technology use habits or decisions, in- service professional development level, teacher–student relationships, personal characteristics, and pedagogical alignment (e.g., Chai et al. 2013; Charania et  al.  2024; Cheng and Xie  2018; Koh et  al.  2014; Ronfeldt et  al.  2013; Tondeur et  al.  2017; Yue et  al.  [2024)](#appendix). In AI- Ed instructional environments, the literature frequently em- phasises that the relationship between teachers' pedagogical competencies and their levels of TK, pedagogical beliefs, and intentions to use technology involves a reciprocal and bidi- rectional interaction (Canbazoğlu Bilici et al. [2024;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Hava and Babayiğit 2025; Karataş and Yüce 2024; Tondeur et al. 2017). However, how this interaction is structured and which indi- vidual and contextual variables play a determining role in these processes are still examined to a limited extent in the current research. In this context, a study conducted by Ning et al. (2025) with 1518 teachers, grounded in the stimulus–or- ganism–response (SOR) theory, examined the impact of school support on teachers' psychological resilience, self- efficacy, at- titudes toward AI, and acceptance of AI; the findings demon- strated that these cognitive factors significantly enhanced AI literacy. Moreover, it was found that AI anxiety had negative effects on these cognitive factors, although its direct impact on AI literacy was not statistically significant. These findings 

3 of 27

highlight the critical role of teachers' affective and cognitive states in the development of technology- related competencies and provide an important reference point for understanding how individual–contextual interactions contribute to AI- based instructional competencies.

The study assumes that teacher collaboration may play a determining role in the development of AI- TPACK compo- nents. This assumption is consistent with previous research indicating that practices such as peer interaction, interper- sonal engagement, experiential sharing, collective knowledge construction, engagement in professional learning actions, co- planning of lessons, and shared reflection contribute sig- nificantly to the development of PK domains grounded in both traditional and AI- Ed instruction (Carlson et al. [2019;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Chai et al. 2013; Koh et al. 2014; Prestridge 2019; Yeh et al. 2021). Teachers who actively engage in collaboration not only share knowledge about instructional materials, but also exchange ideas regarding the integration of innovative technologies such as AI into pedagogical scenarios, their functionality within learning environments, their strengths and limita- tions, and strategic approaches for their use. In this regard, collaborative professional learning communities provide an environment that fosters mutual support, learning through trial and error, and reflective dialogue—elements that are critical for the development of areas such as AI- TK, AI- TPK, and AI- TCK (Hwang et al. 2020; Karataş and Yüce 2024; Lan et al. 2025; Runge et al. 2025). However, despite this theoreti- cal foundation, empirical studies that directly link teacher col- laboration to specific AI- TPACK subdomains remain scarce. Therefore, considering teacher collaboration as a mediating factor in the development of AI- Ed instructional competencies is regarded as one of the original contributions of this study to the literature.

In this study, teacher enthusiasm is conceptualised as a central affective and motivational construct within instructional envi- ronments and is modelled in a multilayered structure based on both knowledge- based and contextual variables. The rationale behind this approach is that teacher enthusiasm is not merely an individual disposition but rather a multidimensional con- struct that exerts a significant influence on the effective use of pedagogical competencies, professional interaction, intrinsic motivation toward subject matter and pedagogical processes, and willingness to integrate innovative technologies. In this context, it is anticipated that teacher enthusiasm will manifest at varying levels in relation to PK, CK, PCK, and technology- related knowledge components involving AI- Ed. Furthermore, a theoretical framework has been adopted in which teacher en- thusiasm is shaped by contextual variables such as individuals' ICT competencies, experiences with AI technologies, and the intensity of their technology use. Previous studies suggest that although technical skills and digital experiences are necessary, they may be insufficient to enhance professional enthusiasm unless supported by pedagogical value attribution and collab- orative practices (Kasalak and Dagyar 2020; Keller et al. 2016; Lan et  al.  2025; Mishra et  al.  2023; Tondeur et  al.  2016; Yue et al. [2024)](#appendix). When evaluated from the perspectives of both SCT and the TAM, these findings highlight the impact of the dy- namic relationship between cognitive competencies and envi- ronmental interactions on teacher motivation.

4 of 27

Gender has increasingly emerged as a salient moderating variable in recent research on technology integration, with evidence suggesting that gender- related differences may sig- nificantly influence teachers' technology- related experiences, usage patterns, pedagogical integration approaches, and per- ceptions of the integration process. The influence of gender is not confined to teachers' competency levels related to AI; it may also affect collaboration patterns, pedagogical prefer- ences, and forms of affective engagement. For instance, the study conducted by Charania et al. (2024) found that female teachers reported higher levels of perceived usefulness and ease of use regarding AI- supported instructional tools com- pared to their male counterparts, while male teachers re- ported greater autonomy and experience in technology use. Similarly, the study by Yue et al. ([2024)](#appendix) reported that although significant differences were observed in TPACK- related fac- tors favouring male teachers, no meaningful difference was identified in perceived importance or interest regarding AI instruction. In the study conducted by Cheng and Xie (2018), male teachers scored significantly higher than female teach- ers in TK, TCK, and TPK dimensions. In this context, the in- clusion of gender as a moderating variable in the present study aims to systematically examine potential differences in how male and female teachers construct and enact their AI- TPACK competencies and teacher enthusiasm.

**2 \| Conceptual and Theoretical Framework**

**2.1 \| Theoretical Framework**

The structural model developed in this study is grounded in two fundamental psychological approaches—Social Cognitive Theory (SCT) and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)—which ex- plain individuals' pedagogical behaviours on both cognitive and social levels. These two theoretical approaches enable a holistic understanding of the relationships among teachers' individual characteristics, professional interaction practices, and their per- ceptions, competencies, and affective outcomes related to technol- ogy. SCT explains individuals' behaviours within the framework of reciprocal interactions among personal factors, environmental in- fluences, and behavioural outcomes (Bandura [1986,](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) [1989;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Schunk and DiBenedetto 2020). This theoretical foundation is employed in the study to explain how teachers' personal attributes relate to professional collaboration, a form of environmental interaction. In particular, the relationship between teachers' self- efficacy per- ceptions (e.g., confidence in professional knowledge, willingness to share) and their level of collaboration aligns directly with the principle of reciprocal determinism in SCT (Pajares 1996; Schunk and DiBenedetto  2020). Similarly, this theoretical framework contributes to understanding how teachers' pedagogical knowl- edge domains are shaped through collaborative, environmentally driven interactions. Collaborative processes such as knowledge sharing, experience exchange, and joint practice among teachers provide a social learning environment that facilitates the develop- ment of their pedagogical and technological competencies—par- ticularly in AI- integrated knowledge domains (Carlson et al. [2019;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Charania et al. 2024; Cheng and Xie 2018; Karataş and Yüce 2024; Lan et al. 2025; Teo 2011). This phenomenon aligns with the core principles of SCT, which emphasise the decisive role of environ- mental factors in individual learning processes.

_European Journal of Education,_ 2025

The core component of this study, AI- TPACK, is conceptualised not merely as a technical competence but as a holistic construct that integrates teachers' cognitive evaluations and pedagogical intentions. In this context, the TAM explains how teachers' ten- dencies to use AI tools are shaped by their perceptions of the usefulness and ease of use of these technologies (Davis 1989; Ursavaş 2022; Ursavaş et al. 2025; Venkatesh and Davis 2000). The development of components such as AI- TK, AI- TCK, AI- TPK, and AI- TPACK is directly linked not only to teachers' tech- nical exposure to these technologies but also to their cognitive appraisal and acceptance of the pedagogical value of AI tools (Mishra et al. 2023; Runge et al. 2025). TAM is also closely as- sociated with affective outcomes. When teachers perceive AI technologies as pedagogically meaningful, accessible, and effec- tive, it shapes not only their intention to use these tools but also forms of emotional engagement such as professional enthusiasm (Keller et al. 2016; Teo 2011). In this regard, teacher enthusi- asm is conceptualised not merely as an individual emotion but as a multidimensional outcome nourished by constructs such as pedagogical competence, usage experience, and professional collaboration.

The contextual factors included in the model hold transforma- tive significance from the perspectives of both SCT and the TAM. According to SCT, such environmental inputs have the capacity to shape both individuals' knowledge structures and their affec- tive motivation (Bandura [1997)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-). According to TAM, these vari- ables influence perceptions of the ease of use and functionality of technology, thereby contributing directly to both behavioural and emotional outcomes (Davis 1989; Ning et al. 2025; Runge et al. 2025). This theoretical framework presents a multi- level structure that explains how teachers' individual and contextual characteristics are transformed into cognitive competencies through professional interactions, and how these competencies, in turn, lead to affective outcomes.

**2.2 \| Teacher Characteristics in AI- Integrated Pedagogy**

Teachers' individual characteristics are among the key de- terminants that shape their pedagogical decision- making processes, classroom practices, collaboration tendencies, and their capacity to effectively integrate digital technologies into instructional environments (Celik  [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Hughes  2012; Ronfeldt et al. 2013). As emphasised in Bandura's ([1986)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) SCT, the direct influence of such individual differences on instruc- tional processes is shaped through the continuous interaction between personal characteristics and environmental factors. Teachers' demographic and professional attributes—such as age, gender, subject area, ethnicity, professional experience, and academic qualifications—affect their attitudes toward technology, participation in collaborative practices, and pro- fessional motivation (Cheng and Xie 2018; Mishra et al. 2023; Nguyen et  al.  2020; Ning et  al.  2025). The meaningful, ef- fective, and sustainable integration of GenAI- based digital technologies into instructional processes is particularly asso- ciated not only with teachers' TPACK competencies but also with their individual characteristics, professional belief sys- tems, and levels of digital competence (Al- Abdullatif  [2024;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Hava and Babayiğit 2025). Therefore, teachers' personal and 

professional characteristics can play a determining role at both cognitive and affective levels in the development of TPACK competencies integrated with GenAI (Charania et  al.  2024; Hwang et al. 2020; Tondeur et al. 2017). For example, teachers' age may influence their processes of adopting and using tech- nology, whereas their teaching experience and belief systems may determine their level of trust in new technologies (Cheng and Xie 2018). Moreover, age and educational level are among the significant individual variables in explaining differences in collaboration among teachers. Previous studies have shown that older and more experienced teachers tend to have lower levels of self- efficacy toward web- based TPACK applications (Lee and Tsai 2010). However, studies conducted in different contexts on the relationship between age and technology in- tegration have yielded inconsistent results (Koh et al. 2014; Yue et al. [2024)](#appendix). On the other hand, the determining effects of teachers' age, instructional level, and value beliefs on their TPACK levels have been clearly demonstrated (Cheng and Xie 2018). These findings indicate that individual character- istics such as age and educational level may affect not only teachers' digital pedagogical competencies but also their ten- dencies toward professional collaboration. Therefore, consid- ering these variables as predictors of teacher collaboration in the present study is strongly supported both theoretically and empirically.

Gender has been shown to have significant effects on participa- tion patterns and levels of interaction, particularly within dig- ital learning environments. For instance, a study by Charania et  al.  (2024) revealed that teachers' levels of participation in GenAI- and TPACK- focused online professional development programmes significantly varied based on individual and con- textual variables such as gender, language preference, digital competence, and teaching experience. This finding suggests that teachers' tendencies to engage in digital learning processes are influenced not only by their technical competencies but also by interactional dynamics shaped by their personal character- istics and professional backgrounds. Teachers' affective traits, such as their approaches to professional collaboration and teach- ing enthusiasm, may differ significantly based on gender; these differences are also reflected in their approaches to technology integration and the motivational dynamics of the instructional process (Tondeur et al. 2017; Yue et al. [2024)](#appendix). Understanding how teacher characteristics interact with AI- TPACK levels and teaching enthusiasm is of critical importance for design- ing a more inclusive and high- quality digital transformation in education. Therefore, analysing teachers' individual char- acteristics through gender- based groupings using multivariate statistical methods will contribute to a deeper understanding of the development of technological competencies and pedagogical commitment.

**2.3 \| Collaboration for Professional Growth in AI- Supported Pedagogy**

Collaboration is a multilayered and dynamic interactive pro- cess in which teachers actively participate in collective learn- ing, innovation, and professional development by sharing their professional knowledge, pedagogical experiences, fu- ture plans, and instructional repertoires. This concept refers 

5 of 27

not only to interpersonal interaction but also to a collective process of production that involves pedagogical decision- making, ensuring continuity in academic progress, contribut- ing to the functionality of collaborative instructional design, and co- constructing innovative practices (Moolenaar  2012; Vangrieken et  al.  2015). Effective collaboration among teachers facilitates the holistic integration of instructional expertise, experiential knowledge, and classroom teaching practices, thereby significantly contributing to the develop- ment of collective capacity and the promotion of professional innovation in instructional processes that aim to integrate digital technologies and AI- supported teaching tools into classroom practice (Koh et al. 2014; Trust and Horrocks 2019; Yildiz Durak [2024)](#appendix). Indeed, the integration of AI- supported teaching tools into classroom practices is a complex process that requires not only technical knowledge but also pedagog- ical and collegial support. In this context, collaboration en- ables teachers to experience the transfer of GenAI- based tools into learning environments not merely as a technical integra- tion process, but as a multifaceted space of transformation in which they deepen their understanding of digital competence and reconstruct their skill- oriented creativity within a frame- work of collective intelligence (Chai et  al.  2013; Chiu and Chai  2020; Prestridge  2019). Collaboration and professional support processes enhance teachers' awareness of GenAI sys- tems, supporting their recognition of intelligent tools specific to their subject areas and their effective use of these tech- nologies for pedagogical purposes (Hwang et  al.  2020; Lan et al. 2025).

Research has shown that collaboration among teachers plays a critical role in the development of TPACK levels and serves as a key mediating factor in making sense of innovative technol- ogies (Koh et al. 2014; Yildiz Durak 2021, 2023) such as GenAI within pedagogical contexts. Moreover, it has been emphasised that teachers who are able to establish effective and sustain- able communication with their colleagues tend to demonstrate higher levels of professional enthusiasm and greater sensitivity toward their students, which in turn significantly strengthens their commitment to the instructional process. In this context, the collaboration variable is addressed in this study as a key con- struct in the analyses aimed at understanding the relationships among teacher characteristics, AI- TPACK, and teaching enthu- siasm, and is examined in conjunction with interaction patterns that differ based on gender.

**2.4 \| AI- Integrated TPACK Components**

Recent studies in literature clearly demonstrate that the TPACK framework has evolved to encompass AI- Ed. This in- novative development reflects the dynamic nature of TPACK and its capacity to adapt to the demands of the digital age. With the increasing prevalence of AI- supported instruc- tional practices, many studies have expanded the scope of the TPACK model by incorporating AI components. Although the studies by Ning et al. (2024), Lorenz and Romeike (2023), Celik ([2023)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-), and Lan et al. (2025) are referred to by different names, they share similar conceptual foundations. Each of them reconstructs the TPACK model by placing AI- Ed at its core, yet they are grounded in the same theoretical foundation (see Figure 1).

AI- TK refers to the fundamental knowledge and skills required for teachers to use AI technologies in educational contexts in a conscious, effective, and critical manner (Celik  [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Lan et al. 2025). It also encompasses a theoretical and practical under- standing of how AI technologies can be meaningfully and effec- tively integrated into instructional processes in accordance with pedagogical principles and strategies (Koehler and Mishra 2009; Mishra et al. 2023; Mishra and Koehler 2006; Ning et al. 2024). AI- TCK refers to teachers' use of AI technologies to design inter- active and engaging learning experiences by taking into account students' knowledge levels, cognitive characteristics, and learn- ing preferences (Ning et al. 2024). It also supports a deeper un- derstanding and more effective delivery of instructional content by enabling teachers to comprehend how GenAI interacts with interdisciplinary content (Lan et al. 2025). Teachers utilise AI to design interactive and meaningful learning experiences tailored to students' needs (Lorenz and Romeike 2023; Ning et al. 2024). AI- TPK refers to the ability to effectively utilise the pedagogical functions of AI tools—such as real- time feedback and learning analytics—and to accurately interpret the feedback provided by these tools (Celik [2023)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-). It reflects teachers' competence in understanding the pedagogical potential of AI technologies and integrating these tools into instructional strategies in a holistic and meaningful way (Mishra et al. 2023). AI- TPACK is a compre- hensive knowledge domain that reflects teachers' ability to inte- grate GenAI technologies with ethical, pedagogical, and CK to innovatively design lesson- based instructional processes, moni- tor learning, provide real- time feedback, and offer equitable and accessible learning opportunities for all students (Celik  [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) 

_European Journal of Education,_ 2025

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Lan et al. 2025; Lorenz and Romeike 2023; Mishra et al. 2023; Ning et al. 2024; Yue et al. [2024)](#appendix). This holistic structure enables teachers to position AI- based technologies not merely as tech- nical tools, but as cognitive and strategic resources that deepen learning, add pedagogical value, and support the construction of inclusive educational environments.

Collaborative work among teachers offers significant op- portunities, particularly for the development of AI- TPACK components. Processes such as joint planning, experience sharing, dissemination of collective knowledge, and co- experimentation with digital tools contribute to a more effec- tive structuring of both technological components and AI- TCK and AI- TPK elements (Chai et  al.  2016; Feldman- Maggor et al. 2025; Moolenaar 2012; Ning et al. 2024; Yeh et al. 2021). Such interactions not only enhance technical competence but also promote openness to instructional innovation, ped- agogical flexibility, and individual professional growth. The relationship between AI- TPACK components and teacher en- thusiasm can be explained by the contribution of these compe- tencies to teaching motivation. In particular, awareness of the ethical and responsible use of AI can strengthen both teach- ers' professional commitment and their processes of subjective meaning- making (Celik [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Lan et al. 2025). Therefore, it is important to consider the ethical dimension not merely as a technical competency but also as a motivational factor that fosters teacher enthusiasm.

**2.5 \| Teacher Enthusiasm in AI- Integrated Pedagogy**

Teacher enthusiasm is recognised as a key teacher character- istic that encompasses the affective dimension of instructional processes and plays a decisive role in both teachers' classroom effectiveness and students' learning motivation (Kasalak and Dagyar  2020). Accordingly, teacher enthusiasm is defined as a holistic manifestation of nonverbal expressions, effective in- teraction patterns, positive emotions rooted in professional competence, and internalised affective experiences that are re- flected in the instructional process (Keller et al. 2016; Kunter et al. 2011). With ongoing technological advancements, teacher enthusiasm has become increasingly important and is emerging as a fundamental element of teacher- student communication in digital learning environments. Indeed, as the primary actor responsible for integrating increasingly prevalent generative AI tools into learning environments, the teacher's role goes beyond mere technological implementation and requires the pedagogi- cally appropriate, meaningful, and sensitive use of these tools. Enthusiastic teachers tend to maintain their motivation to teach and continually seek ways to enhance instructional processes. In this context, teacher enthusiasm positively and directly influ- ences the quality of both teaching and learning processes (Cui et al. 2017). Within the AI- TPACK framework, teacher enthusi- asm is considered a critical affective component that supports not only pedagogical effectiveness but also the meaningful and ethical integration of AI technologies into instructional strate- gies (Lan et al. 2025; Mishra et al. 2023). The use of GenAI tools in lesson design aligned with creative and pedagogical princi- ples enhances teachers' professional motivation and strengthens 

classroom interactions (Yildiz Durak et  al.  [2025)](#appendix). Increased interaction and emotional engagement foster teacher enthusi- asm and positively reflect on the quality of learning environ- ments (Charania et al. 2024; Durak 2023; Frenzel et al. 2009). Accordingly, teachers with high levels of AI- TPACK proficiency tend to adopt AI- based tools not merely as technical applications but as strategic instruments aligned with pedagogical goals, which nurture their desire to teach and deepen interaction with students (Celik [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Mishra et al. 2023; Ning et al. 2024). This reciprocal interaction between teacher enthusiasm and AI- TPACK components holds the potential to structure AI- supported instructional processes in a more holistic, effective, and sustainable manner by addressing both their cognitive and affective dimensions (Lan et al. 2025).

**3 \| Methods**

**3.1 \| Model of the Study**

In this study, an exploratory SEM approach was employed to ex- amine the relationships among teacher characteristics, collab- oration, AI- TPACK components, and teacher enthusiasm. SEM is an advanced statistical technique that allows for a compre- hensive analysis of the relationships between observed variables and latent constructs (Kline  2023). This method enables the simultaneous testing of both measurement models (i.e., the re- lationships between latent constructs and their observed indica- tors) and structural models (i.e., the causal relationships among latent variables) (Schumacker and Lomax 2010). This approach is particularly well- suited for models that involve complex struc- tures and aim to evaluate the effects of mediating variables. The model developed in this study conceptually represents the theoretical relationships among the variables examined in the study. The arrows in the diagram illustrate the causal directions and interaction paths among the variables, while the labels on each arrow correspond to specific hypotheses (H1a, H2c, etc.). This visual arrangement establishes a clear link between the theoretical structure of the model and the statistical testing pro- cess. In this context, the model clarifies structural relationships through SEM.

This model (see Figure 2) is grounded in an integrated theoret- ical perspective that combines SCT and the TAM to explain the multilevel variables shaping teachers' AI- TPACK competencies and affective dispositions. This theoretical structure enables a systematic analysis of the complex relationships among individ- ual and professional characteristics, environmental interaction patterns, and cognitive evaluations. It thus provides a founda- tion for exploring the multilayered causal pathways between variables such as collaboration, technology integration, and teaching enthusiasm.

**3.2.1** \| **SCT As a Framework for AI- Integrated Pedagogical Behaviour**

One of the theoretical foundations of this study is SCT, developed by Albert Bandura ([1986)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-). This theory posits that individuals' behaviours are shaped through the reciprocal interaction among personal characteristics (e.g., age, educational level, belief sys- tems), environmental factors (e.g., professional collaboration, organisational culture), and behavioural outcomes (e.g., level of technology integration, teacher enthusiasm) (Bandura [1989;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Pajares  1996). In this context, teachers' individual and job- related characteristics influence both their digital pedagogical competencies and their levels of AI technology adoption and use (Charania et al. 2024; Cheng and Xie 2018; Sun et al. 2022; Tondeur et al. 2017). Specifically, cognitive mechanisms such as self- efficacy and outcome expectations directly influence teachers' attitudes toward AI- based pedagogical innovations, their motivation for implementation, and their level of profes- sional collaboration (Bandura [1997;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Chen et al. 2020; Chiu and Chai 2020; Schunk and DiBenedetto 2020). Within the frame- work of SCT, effective collaboration with colleagues contributes to the development of teachers' PK related to AI technologies (e.g., AI- TK, AI- TPK, AI- TCK) and facilitates the integration of this knowledge with affective outcomes including teaching en- thusiasm (Lan et al. 2025; Prestridge 2019). This aligns directly with the theoretical principles suggesting that individuals can enhance their behavioural capacity through environmental sup- port (e.g., professional communities, access to digital resources).

**3.2.2** \| **TAM and Its Cognitive Foundations in AI- Integrated Pedagogy**

The second theoretical foundation of this study is the TAM and contemporary technology acceptance approaches devel- oped based on this model. Developed by Davis (1989), TAM posits that individuals' intentions to use a new technology are determined by two key cognitive variables: perceived use- fulness and perceived ease of use. In subsequent studies, the model has been expanded to include variables such as social components, cognitive load, and willingness to use technol- ogy for learning purposes, and has been adapted to various educational contexts (Teo 2011; Venkatesh and Davis 2000). The AI- TPACK framework adapts the principles of TAM to pedagogical contexts by addressing critical questions such as how teachers perceive AI technologies in lesson design, how they evaluate the contribution of these tools to learn- ing processes, and how they implement them in practice (Karataş and Ataç 2024; Runge et al. 2025; Wang et al. 2024). Particularly, teachers' perceptions of the educational value of AI- based tools and their trust in using them play a critical role in shaping their AI- TK and AI- TPACK competencies (Al- Abdullatif [2024;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Hava and Babayiğit 2025; Mishra et al. 2023). Moreover, exploring the link between technology acceptance and affective outcomes—such as teacher enthusiasm—re- quires support from broader models that capture the emo- tional dimensions of attitudes toward technology. This study aims to analyse the relationships among teachers' individual and professional characteristics, collaboration, AI- TPACK, and teaching enthusiasm through a multilevel and holistic

**3.3 \| Participants**

The data for this study were collected through an online survey administered to teachers working across Türkiye. The data col- lection process was conducted in collaboration with volunteer teachers working in different geographic regions and at various school levels across the country. This study was conducted in ac- cordance with the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Prior to data collection, informed consent was ob- tained from all participants, who were assured that their partici- pation was voluntary, their responses would remain anonymous, and that they could withdraw at any stage without consequence. No personally identifiable information was collected.

The target population consisted of teachers working in public or private educational institutions across Türkiye, representing diversity in terms of subject areas and teaching levels. Within the scope of the study, data were collected from a total of 323 teachers representing all seven geographical regions of Türkiye. In this study, purposive sampling was used to recruit partici- pants who had been exposed to AI technologies in educational 

contexts to at least some degree. The rationale for this sampling strategy was to ensure that participants had sufficient back- ground knowledge to meaningfully assess their pedagogical competencies integrated with AI. Data was collected through voluntary participation via professional teacher networks, in- cluding regional WhatsApp groups, academic mailing lists, and communications with school administrators across Türkiye.

According to Table 1, 59.8% of participants were female, 40.2% were male, and the average age was 42.09 (SD = 8.52). The teach- ers' subject areas were highly diverse and were grouped as follows: Physical Education, Computer and Instructional Technologies, Religious Education, Fine Arts (Art/Music), Mathematics and Science, Special Education, Basic Education (Preschool and Primary School), Turkish and Social Sciences, and Foreign Languages. Among the participants, 65.0% held a bachelor's de- gree and 35.0% held a postgraduate degree. The participants had an average of 18.46 years of teaching (professional) experience (SD = 8.83). In terms of school levels, 27.2% of the participants were working in preschool and primary education, 51.4% in mid- dle school, and 21.4% in high school settings. In order to ensure diversity and generalisability across the country, teachers from all regions of Türkiye were included in the study. Türkiye has seven geographical regions. The regional distribution of participants is as follows: Central Anatolia (33.1%), Aegean (32.8%), Marmara

**3.4.2** \| **AI- TPACK Scale**

The AI–TPACK Scale was developed by Ning et al. (2024), and its Turkish adaptation was carried out by Canbazoğlu Bilici et  al.  ([2024)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-). The scale aims to measure teachers' competen- cies in integrating AI- based technologies into instructional processes. The theoretical background of the scale is based on the TPACK model proposed by Mishra and Koehler (2006). The scale includes the dimensions of TK, PK, and CK, as well as the intersecting components derived from these domains: PCK, TCK, TPK, and the integrated domain of TPACK. In addition to these dimensions, the instrument is enriched with items that assess teachers' competencies in AI- specific instructional prac- tices. The scale consists of 39 items and employs a 5- point Likert- type rating structure (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree).

Examples of how the items related to the subdimensions of the AI- TPACK scale used in this study function at the application level are presented in Appendix Table [A.](#appendix) Each item is explained in terms of the type of AI tool or application practice with which it can be associated in teaching environments, beyond the sub- dimension on which it is theoretically based.

**3.4.3** \| **Teacher Enthusiasm Scale**

The Teacher Enthusiasm Scale was developed to assess teach- ers' levels of teaching enthusiasm and subject enthusiasm. The scale was originally constructed by Kunter et  al.  (2011), and its Turkish adaptation was carried out by Kasalak and Dagyar  (2020). The scale consists of 10 items and comprises two subdimensions: (i) teaching enthusiasm and (ii) subject enthusiasm. The scale is structured using a 5- point Likert- type 

rating system (1 = Strongly Disagree, 5 = Strongly Agree). The teaching enthusiasm subdimension reflects the teacher's intrin- sic motivation toward the instructional process, the enjoyment derived from delivering lessons and conveying new knowledge, 

**3.4.4** \| **Teacher Collaboration Scale**

multidimensional approach to teacher collaboration, consid- ering both the content domain and the nature of interaction. Accordingly, the scale consists of two primary content dimen-

laboration (e.g., sharing teaching materials, discussing lesson content) and school- related collaboration (e.g., participating in school development activities, discussing team development)” were addressed. The scale items reflect the various types of col- laboration that teachers engage in with their colleagues: shar- ing teaching materials, discussing assessment criteria, sharing lesson content, observing lessons, discussing lesson design, team teaching, planning participation in training, sharing conference information, sharing new learning, discussing the implementation of the school program, participating in school development activities, and team development discussions. These items encompass both low- cost (e.g., material sharing) and high- cost (e.g., team teaching, lesson observation) types of collaboration. Collaborative activities related to teaching, par- ticularly lesson material sharing and lesson design discussions, can directly support teachers' ability to integrate AI- based tools (e.g., learning analytics platforms, AI- supported simulations) into pedagogical processes. For example, teachers discussing lesson content design using an AI- based tool can promote the development of AI- TCK and AI- TPK components. Similarly, high- cost collaboration types such as lesson observation and team teaching can enable teachers to deepen their AI- TPACK competencies by observing and applying the pedagogical ef- fects of AI tools. School- related collaborative activities, such as discussions on the implementation of the school program or activities aimed at school development, can contribute to the development of AI- TPACK in a broader context by supporting the integration of AI technologies at the institutional level. The frequency of teachers' participation in collaborative activities is an important factor in determining the impact of these ac- tivities. Although the original version of the scale was devel- oped using a 4- point Likert- type format, a 5- point Likert- type response scale (1 = Never, 5 = Always) was employed in this study. More frequent low- cost activities such as sharing teach- ing materials can contribute to teachers' development of basic technological knowledge such as AI- TK. In contrast, although high- cost activities such as lesson observation or team teaching

**3.5 \| Data Analysis**

In this section, the validity study of the scales was first con- ducted using Lisrel 8.0, and the findings are presented below. Information regarding data analysis is then provided. According to the confirmatory factor analysis and expert opinions con- ducted for the Teacher Collaboration Scale, the factor loadings of the items in the scale ranged from 0.50 to 0.76, except for Item 1. Hair et al. (2017) stated that these values are threshold values of 

0.4 and above, which are considered acceptable and satisfactory. Item 1 fell below the 0.4 value, and two expert opinions were sought regarding whether this item should remain in the model. Experts in the field of Computer and Instructional Technologies expressed their opinion that the item should remain. Therefore, the item was not removed from the scale. Chi- square and de- grees of freedom values were examined to evaluate model fit. The Cronbach's alpha values calculated for the factors in the scale were 0.862 for “instructional- related collaboration” and 0.905 for “school- related collaboration.” These findings provide sufficient evidence of the scale's reliability.

According to the confirmatory factor analysis conducted for the Teacher Enthusiasm Scale, the factor loadings of the items in the scale ranged between 0.50 and 0.54. Therefore, the item was not removed from the scale. Chi- square and degrees of freedom values were examined to evaluate model fit. The Cronbach's alpha values calculated for the factors in the scale were 0.942 for “teaching enthusiasm” and 0.950 for “subject enthusi- asm.” These findings provide sufficient evidence of the scale's reliability.

Data analysis was conducted using Partial Least Squares–SEM (PLS- SEM), a non- parametric SEM technique. The analysis was performed using the SmartPLS 4 software. PLS- SEM is a modelling approach with high assumption flexibility that en- ables the examination of relationships between dependent and independent variables in models involving multivariate struc- tures (Gefen et al. 2000). Additionally, to investigate whether the structural paths differed based on gender, the sample was divided into subgroups (male and female teachers), and Multi- Group Analysis (MGA) was conducted. Within the scope of the MGA, path coefficients were compared for each group, and the statistical significance of these differences was evaluated.

**4 \| Results**

During the testing process of the measurement model, outer loadings, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discrim- inant validity were analysed sequentially to assess the validity and reliability of the constructs in the model. First, the outer loading values indicating the contribution of each observed vari- able to its corresponding latent construct were examined. In the relevant literature, the acceptable threshold for outer loadings is 

12 of 27

typically set at 0.70 or above (Hair, Sarstedt, et al. 2019). Internal consistency reliability was assessed using both Cronbach's alpha coefficient and composite reliability values. For both indicators, values of 0.70 or higher indicate that the construct possesses high internal consistency (Hair, Sarstedt, et al. 2019; Jöreskog 1978). Convergent validity was examined based on the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) values for each construct. AVE rep- resents the average amount of variance explained by the con- struct, and the minimum acceptable threshold in the literature is 0.50 (Hair, Sarstedt, et al. 2019). Values exceeding this thresh- old indicate that the items on the scale adequately represent the corresponding construct. In cases where the model includes conceptually similar constructs, discriminant validity analy- sis becomes critically important. The Heterotrait–Monotrait Ratio (HTMT) method proposed by Henseler et al. (2015) was employed. An HTMT value below 0.90 supports the discrimin- ability of constructs and confirms the validity of the measure- ment model.

**4.1 \| Common Method Bias**

The full collinearity method proposed by Kock (2015) was used for common factor bias. The relationship between the struc- tures in the measurement model and a common variable was examined. In this context, the VIF values were below 10 (see Hair et al. 2013; Hair, Risher, et al. 2019). As shown in Appendix Table B, the findings indicate that common method bias did not threaten the findings.

**4.2 \| Evaluation of the Measurement Model: Reliability and Validity Analysis**

This section evaluates the validity and reliability of the measure- ment model for the latent variables included in the hypothesised structural model. First, the outer loading coefficients, which in- dicate the loading of each observed variable on its correspond- ing subdimension, were examined. The findings presented in Appendix Table C demonstrate that all constructs included in the model exhibit high loading values. When examining the subfactors of the AI- TPACK scale, the outer loading values of the items in the PK dimension range from 0.800 to 0.881, while those in the CK dimension range from 0.827 to 0.893, indicating that both dimensions exhibit a high level of reliability. The load- ing values in the AI- TK dimension range from 0.912 to 0.949, suggesting that this dimension is strongly represented and demonstrates high internal consistency. The values related to the PCK subdimension range from 0.700 to 0.891, indicating that all items fall within acceptable thresholds in terms of validity. The outer loading values in the AI- TCK dimension range from 0.880 to 0.956, while those in the AI- TPK dimension range from 0.960 to 0.971, indicating that both dimensions demonstrate very high levels of reliability. The loadings of the items related to the integrated structure of AI- TPACK range from 0.866 to 0.959, demonstrating that the construct possesses high validity and re- liability. Regarding the teacher collaboration variable, the outer loading values for the educational collaboration subdimension range from 0.606 to 0.821, while those for the school- related col- laboration subdimension range from 0.720 to 0.850. The lowest loading value, 0.606 (item TC6), meets the minimum acceptable 

_European Journal of Education,_ 2025

threshold of 0.60 (Hair, Sarstedt, et al. 2019), indicating that the item remains valid. An examination of the teacher enthusiasm instrument reveals that the loading values for the teaching en- thusiasm subdimension range from 0.820 to 0.895, while those for the subject enthusiasm subdimension range from 0.836 to 0.901, indicating that both dimensions exhibit high levels of re- liability. All these findings indicate that the observed variables included in the model largely exhibit outer loading values above the recommended threshold of 0.70, thereby confirming that the measurement model is reliable in terms of both construct valid- ity and internal consistency.

Table 3 presents the findings from the construct reliability and convergent validity analyses conducted for the constructions included in the study. In this context, Cronbach's alpha, along with the composite reliability indicators rho\_a and rho\_c, was calculated to assess the construct reliability.

An examination of Table 3 reveals that all construct reliability and convergent validity indicators calculated for constructions included in the study meet the recommended threshold values. Indeed, all values of Cronbach's alpha and composite reliabil- ity coefficients (rho\_a and rho\_c) calculated for construct reli- ability exceed the commonly accepted threshold. This indicates that the constructs exhibit a high level of internal consistency. In particular, the Cronbach's alpha values for AI- TPK (0.986), AI- TPACK (0.966), AI- TCK (0.970), and teacher enthusiasm (0.965) exceed 0.950, demonstrating that these constructs are exceptionally reliable in terms of measurement. Furthermore, the convergent validity of the constructs was assessed based on the AVE values, which represent the shared variance among the items belonging to each construct. All constructs exceed the rec- ommended threshold for AVE. Specifically, constructs such as AI- TPK (0.933), AI- TPACK (0.881), and AI- TCK (0.871) exhibit notably high AVE values, indicating that these constructs are conceptually strong and consistently represented. On the other hand, although teacher collaboration (0.593) and PCK (0.689) exhibit relatively lower AVE values, they still meet the mini- mum threshold and support the overall validity structure of the model. Overall, it can be concluded that all latent variables in the model demonstrate both high reliability and satisfactory convergent validity.

**Measured constructs** **Cronbach's alpha**

Table 4 presents the HTMT values calculated among the con- structs included in the study. This analysis was conducted to evaluate discriminant validity by testing the extent to which each construct can be statistically distinguished from the others. In the literature, the commonly accepted upper limit for HTMT values is 0.850 or 0.900 (Henseler et al. 2015). Exceeding these thresholds indicates weak discriminability between the con- structs and suggests a potential risk of overlap.

According to Table 4, relatively high levels of association were observed among certain constructs. For instance, HTMT val- ues of 0.916 between AI- TK and AI- TCK, 0.900 between AI- TK and AI- TPK, and 0.890 between AI- TCK and AI- TPK were ob- tained. These findings suggest that the subdimensions related to AI technologies exhibit theoretical overlaps, necessitating more cautious interpretation of the measurement model with respect to these constructs. Values such as 0.757 between PK and PCK, and 0.469 between teacher enthusiasm and PCK indi- cate that discriminant validity is preserved for these constructs. Additionally, HTMT values such as 0.679 between AI usage ex- perience and AI usage intensity, and 0.601 between AI usage experience and AI- TK, demonstrate moderate correlations that align with the expected theoretical orientation. However, the study conducted by Henseler et  al.  (2015) indicates that values below 1 threshold are acceptable (poor), which shows that measurement- based differentiation between structures is achieved.

**4.3 \| Structural Model Evaluation and Hypothesis Testing**

Following the validation of the measurement model, the struc- tural model was evaluated through the PLS- SEM method to test the proposed research model and hypotheses. In evaluating the model, the coefficient of determination (_R_2), which indicates the explained variance of the dependent variables, was taken as the primary criterion. The _R_2 value is a statistical measure ranging between 0 and 1, indicating the proportion of variance in the de- pendent variable that is explained by the independent variables included in the model. A high _R_2 value indicates that the model has a high level of explanatory power (Hair et al. 2021).

An examination of Table  5 reveals that the _R_2 values of the endogenous variables in the structural model are generally at low levels. The highest _R_2 value, 0.259, belongs to the teacher enthusiasm construct. This indicates that the model explains approximately 25.9% of the variance in teacher enthusiasm and that its effect on this variable is more substantial compared to other constructs. This construct is followed by PCK (0.142), CK (0.114), and PK (0.099), respectively. These values indicate that the model has a limited yet noteworthy explanatory power regarding these variables. On the other hand, the _R_2 values for AI- based knowledge components such as AI- TCK (0.039), AI- TPACK (0.034), AI- TPK (0.032), and AI- TK (0.022) are no- tably low. This finding suggests that the model's explanatory power over these constructs is limited and that the variance in these components is largely determined by factors outside the model. The lowest _R_2 value, 0.008, is associated with the teacher collaboration variable, indicating that the model has a weak explanatory power for this construct. The path coef- ficients, standard deviations, _t_- values, and hypothesis testing results related to the SEM were analysed to evaluate the effect of each independent variable on the corresponding dependent variable and to determine the statistical significance of these effects (see Table 6).

According to Table 6, the teacher collaboration variable has significant and positive effects on various domains of knowl- edge. Specifically, the effects observed on PK (_β_ = 0.314, _t_ = 5.062, _p_ \< 0.001), CK (_β_ = 0.338, _t_ = 5.246, _p_ \< 0.001), AI- TK (_β_ = 0.150, _t_ = 2.213, _p_ \< 0.05), PCK (_β_ = 0.377, _t_ = 6.398, _p_ \< 0.001), AI- TCK (_β_ = 0.198, _t_ = 3.002, _p_ \< 0.01), AI- TPK (_β_ = 0.178, _t_ = 2.664, _p_ \< 0.01) and AI- TPACK (_β_ = 0.185, _t_ = 2.787, _p_ \< 0.01) suggest that teacher collaboration contrib- utes not only to traditional PK components but also to AI- integrated TPACK domains. This indicates that professional interaction and collaboration play a significant role in the development of teachers' technology- enhanced instructional competencies. With regard to the predictors of teacher en- thusiasm, significant relationships were found only with PK (_β_ = 0.183, _t_ = 2.130, _p_ \< 0.05), AI- TK (_β_ = 0.259, _t_ = 1.975, _p_ \< 0.05) and PCK (_β_ = 0.252, _t_ = 2.468, _p_ \< 0.05). Other knowl- edge constructs—CK (_β_ = 0.071, _t_ = 0.692, _p_ \> 0.05), AI- TCK (_β_ = −0.168, _t_ = 0.801, _p_ \> 0.05), AI- TPK (_β_ = 0.200, _t_ = 0.857,

_p_ \> 0.05), and AI- TPACK (_β_ = −0.119, _t_ = 0.611, _p_ \> 0.05)—did not exhibit statistically significant effects on teacher enthusi- asm. These findings suggest that teacher enthusiasm is pri- marily informed by pedagogical and content- based constructs such as PK, PCK, and AI- TK, whereas AI- based knowledge domains may be insufficient in establishing a direct relation- ship with such affective outcomes. Additionally, the lack of significant relationships between teacher enthusiasm and educational ICT usage competence (_β_ = −0.004, _t_ = 0.067, _p_ \> 0.05), AI usage experience (_β_ = 0.000, _t_ = 0.008, _p_ \> 0.05), and AI usage intensity (_β_ = −0.087, _t_ = 1.598, _p_ \> 0.05) suggests that individual technology- related experiences do not directly translate into higher levels of professional enthusiasm among teachers. Finally, the effects of individual and professional demographic variables on teacher collaboration were also ex- amined; it was found that age (_β_ = −0.034, _t_ = 0.258, _p_ \> 0.05), educational level (_β_ = 0.001, _t_ = 0.011, _p_ \> 0.05), professional experience (_β_ = 0.106, _t_ = 0.799, _p_ \> 0.05), and school type (_β_ = −0.046, _t_ = 0.769, _p_ \> 0.05) were not statistically signifi- cant predictors. This result suggests that teacher collaboration is shaped more by organisational or contextual factors rather than by demographic characteristics. It can be seen that _f_2 val- ues show weak and moderate effects in meaningful paths.

Figure 3 visually presents the standardised path coefficients and the significance levels of these paths in the SEM tested in the study. The thickness of the path lines has been dynamically adjusted based on the corre- sponding coefficient values, thereby visually emphasising the strength of each effect. In this way, the interactions between the constructs in the model have been made interpretable not only numerically but also visually.

According to Figure 3, the rejection of hypotheses H1a, H1b, H1c, and H1d indicates that the variables of age, educational level, professional experience, and school type do not have a significant effect on teacher collaboration. These findings suggest that collaboration behaviours are shaped more by con- textual or organisational dynamics rather than by individual characteristics. On the other hand, the acceptance of all hy- potheses from H2a to H2g demonstrates that teacher collab- oration has strong and significant effects on both TPACK and AI- TPACK components. These findings support the idea that as the level of interaction among teachers increases, their com- petencies in integrating AI into instructional processes also

**4.4 \| MGA For Gender- Based Comparisons**

Within the scope of the model- related findings, subgroups were created based on gender, and an MGA was conducted to test the statistical significance of differences between groups. In the MGA process, it is recommended to first test measurement invariance to ensure that group- based models are comparable and that latent variables are represented simi- larly across groups (Henseler et al. 2015). During the analysis process, the explanatory power of the structural model (_R_2), predictive relevance (_Q_2), and effect size (_f_2) were tested for both subgroups. Subsequently, difference analyses were per- formed using the MGA method to evaluate the comparability of path coefficients between groups. Based on the specified grouping variable, the data were divided into subsets, and sep- arate bootstrapping procedures were applied for each group. The sampling distributions obtained at this stage were com- paratively evaluated within the framework of MGA, and the structural paths were statistically tested for significant differ- ences based on gender.

16 of 27

According to Table 7, the MGA results by gender groups re- veal similarities between male and female teachers in certain constructs, while some paths are found to be significant only within specific groups. Among the predictors of the teacher collaboration variable, PK, CK, and PCK emerged as sig- nificant paths in both the female and male groups: PK (fe- male: _β_ = 0.361, _t_ = 4.892, _p_ \< 0.001; male: _β_ = 0.311, _t_ = 2.765, _p_ \< 0.01), CK (female: _β_ = 0.372, _t_ = 5.509, _p_ \< 0.001; male: _β_ = 0.316, _t_ = 2.753, _p_ \< 0.01), and PCK (female: _β_ = 0.388, _t_ = 5.830, _p_ \< 0.001; male: _β_ = 0.378, _t_ = 3.808, _p_ \< 0.001). This finding indicates that teacher collaboration is consistently associated with pedagogical and content knowledge- based constructs regardless of gender. In terms of the teacher enthu- siasm variable, significant paths differ between gender groups. For example, PK emerged as a significant predictor only in the female group (_β_ = 0.327, _t_ = 3.520, _p_ \< 0.001), while it was not found to be significant in the male group (_β_ = 0.125, _t_ = 0.530, _p_ \> 0.05). Similarly, AI- TK is significant only in the male group (_β_ = 0.260, _t_ = 1.977, _p_ \< 0.05), whereas this relationship is not statistically significant in the female group (_β_ = 0.203, _t_ = 828,

_p_ \> 0.05). Moreover, the fact that knowledge components such as CK, PCK, AI- TCK, AI- TPK, and AI- TPACK did not show a significant relationship (_p_ \> 0.05) with teacher enthusiasm in either gender group suggests that only certain pedagogical or technological components have an influence on affective out- comes. On the other hand, educational ICT usage competence, AI usage experience, and AI usage intensity were not found to have a significant effect (_p_ \> 0.05) on teacher enthusiasm in either group.

According to Figures 4 and 5, although the relationships be- tween teacher collaboration and AI- TPACK components are generally similar across gender groups, significant differences were observed in certain dimensions. The teacher collabora- tion variable was found to have significant and positive effects on PK (H2a), CK (H2b), PCK (H2d), and AI- TPACK (H2g) in both the female and male subsamples. However, the fact that the relationships between teacher collaboration and AI- TCK (H2e) and AI- TPK (H2f) were found to be significant only in the female group suggests that collaboration- based interac- tions among female teachers may be more strongly associated with the development of AI- TPACK. When examining the effects of AI- TPACK components on teacher enthusiasm, PK (H3a) emerges as a significant predictor only in the female group, while AI- TK (H3c) is a significant predictor only in the male group. This differentiation suggests that PK is effective in enhancing female teachers' professional motivation, whereas technology- based knowledge plays a more decisive role among male teachers. In contrast, the lack of significant relationships between CK (H3b), PCK (H3d), AI- TCK (H3e), AI- TPK (H3f), and AI- TPACK (H3g) and teacher enthusiasm in either group indicates that these knowledge components do not exert a strong direct influence on affective outcomes. Furthermore, the contextual variables—ICT usage competence (H4a), AI 

usage experience (H4b), and AI usage intensity (H4c)—do not show significant effects on teacher enthusiasm in either the female or male group. These findings indicate that indi- vidual technology usage competencies and experiences do not directly affect teachers' professional enthusiasm.

**5 \| Discussion**

**5.1 \| Overview of Key Findings**

In this study, the relationships among teacher characteristics, collaboration, AI- TPACK, and teacher enthusiasm were ex- amined within the framework of a multilevel model and com- paratively evaluated through MGA in the context of gender differences. The findings have provided important insights into the effects of both individual and contextual variables on educa- tional outcomes.

According to the findings of the structural model, age (H1a), educational level (H1b), professional experience (H1c), and school type (H1d) did not significantly predict teachers' levels of professional collaboration. This finding is consistent with Bandura's ([1986)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) principle of reciprocal determinism within SCT, suggesting that environmental and contextual factors may be more influential than the direct effects of individual variables (Cheng and Xie 2018; Tondeur et al. 2017). Similarly, the influence of gender, digital competence, and contex- tual interactions on collaboration processes emphasised by Charania et  al.  (2024) and Yue et  al.  ([2024)](#appendix) supports these findings. Teacher collaboration demonstrates significant and positive effects on both traditional TPACK components and AI- Ed components. This finding aligns with assertions that collaborative practices—such as co- planning, peer learning,
