collective reflection, and experience sharing—not only sup- port teachers' pedagogical development but also enhance their competence in strategically integrating AI tools into instruc- tional design (Chai et al. 2013; Karataş and Yüce 2024; Koh et al. 2014; Lan et al. 2025; Runge et al. 2025; Yeh et al. 2021). Especially considering the multidimensional structure of the AI- TPACK framework, collaboration has the potential not only to enhance teachers' technical competencies but also to transform their pedagogical perspectives (Celik [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Mishra et al. 2023; Ning et al. 2024).

PK, PCK, and AI- TK components were found to have signifi- cantly predictive effects on teacher enthusiasm. In contrast, CK, AI- TCK, AI- TPK, and AI- TPACK components did not significantly predict teacher enthusiasm. This result indicates that pedagogically grounded types of knowledge are partic- ularly influential in fostering teacher enthusiasm. The find- ing that AI- TK significantly predicts teacher enthusiasm only among male teachers aligns with previous studies suggesting that male teachers tend to demonstrate higher levels of AI- TK (Hava and Babayiğit 2025; Karataş and Ataç 2024). This find- ing highlights the importance of considering gender- based differences when examining affective outcomes such as atti- tudes toward technology and enthusiasm (Al- Abdullatif [2024;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Runge et al. 2025; Yildiz Durak [2024)](#appendix). The lack of significant effects from variables such as ICT usage in education, AI experience, and usage intensity on teacher enthusiasm sug- gests that the influence of technology integration on affective outcomes cannot be fully explained solely through techni- cal competencies. This suggests that teacher enthusiasm is shaped more profoundly by cognitive processes such as ped- agogical value attribution and professional meaning- making (Lan et al. 2025; Mishra et al. 2023).

**5.2 \| Teacher Collaboration and AI- TPACK Components**

The research findings revealed that teacher collaboration significantly predicts all components of the AI- TPACK framework. This indicates that collaboration is not limited to knowledge exchange, but also emphasises the necessity of using digital tools effectively and meaningfully for instruc- tional purposes. Specifically, Chiu and Chai (2020) and Mishra et al. (2023) argue that collaboration provides a context that stimulates teachers' higher- order cognitive processes, thereby facilitating the effective development of TPACK components. The findings show that teachers develop their competencies in integrating AI technologies into pedagogical processes not only through individual expertise but also through the collective interaction networks they establish with their col- leagues. Collaboration in the development of technically oriented components such as AI- TK, AI- TCK, and AI- TPK facilitates teachers' hands- on experience with these tech- nologies and contributes to strengthening their professional self- confidence. In this way, teachers have the opportunity to develop not only their technical skills but also their pedagogi- cal competencies tailored to students' learning needs through interaction- based practices such as material development, joint lesson planning, idea exchange, and experience sharing. From the perspective of SCT, collaboration lies at the core of teachers' processes of gaining behavioural capacity through environmental support. Such support not only aims to provide access to knowledge but also encourages active participation in interpreting, restructuring, analysing, and applying that knowledge. Therefore, the development of AI- TPACK compe- tencies becomes possible not solely through individual effort, but also through interaction- driven learning processes and 

19 of 27

the dynamics of professional communities. In conclusion, the findings of this study reveal that teacher collaboration serves as a central factor not only in shaping technical competencies in AI- supported instructional design but also in enabling the cognitive processes that drive pedagogical transformation. This reflects a paradigm shift in which teacher professional- ism is deepened not through individual knowledge accumu- lation alone, but through collective intelligence and shared experiences.

**5.3 \| Teacher Enthusiasm and AI- TPACK, Pedagogical, and Contextual Components**

The findings of the study reveal that the levels of PK, PCK, and AI- TK have significant predictive effects on teacher enthusiasm. This finding reflects the strong relationship between teacher enthusiasm and pedagogical competence. The findings directly align with SCT. According to this theory, individuals' behaviours are shaped through the reciprocal interaction among personal characteristics, environmental factors, and behavioural out- comes (Bandura [1997;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Schunk and DiBenedetto 2020). Within this framework, teachers' pedagogical skills, technology use competencies, and environmental supports become key in- puts that nurture teacher enthusiasm. Indeed, processes in which teachers collaboratively learn, apply, and contextualise technology with their colleagues enhance not only cognitive development but also emotional engagement (Celik [2023;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Lan et al. 2025; Ning et al. 2024; Prestridge 2019). However, the ab- sence of significant effects of constructs such as CK, AI- TCK, AI- TPK, and AI- TPACK on teacher enthusiasm suggests that acquiring technology or CK alone does not generate an effective response. From the perspective of the TAM (Davis 1989), this result indicates that variables such as perceived ease of use or technical proficiency alone are insufficient to determine teacher enthusiasm. Enthusiasm is more likely shaped by evaluations such as perceived usefulness and pedagogical alignment (Al- Abdullatif [2024;](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) Runge et al. 2025). In terms of contextual vari- ables, the lack of significant effects of ICT usage competence, AI usage experience, and usage intensity on teacher enthusi- asm suggests that such factors remain limited to the technical domain and do not directly contribute to the process of peda- gogical meaning- making. These findings suggest that teacher enthusiasm is shaped not only by technical proficiency but also by processes of pedagogical value attribution (Feldman- Maggor et al. 2025; Hava and Babayiğit 2025). On the other hand, gender- based analyses reveal that PK significantly predicts teacher en- thusiasm only among female teachers, whereas AI- TK does so only among male teachers, indicating that the affective reflec- tions of pedagogical and technological knowledge types differ by gender. This finding underscores the importance of structur- ing teacher support systems in a gender- sensitive manner with respect to both pedagogical and technological dimensions.

It is also noteworthy that certain knowledge components did not exhibit significant effects on teacher enthusiasm in this study. The study found that the effects of CK, AI- TCK, AI- TPK, and AI- TPACK were not statistically significant. This suggests that certain knowledge domains may not be directly associated with teachers' emotional engagement. For example, CK represents a teacher's subject- matter expertise; however, it is not directly 

20 of 27

connected to pedagogical creativity or classroom interaction. Therefore, it may not be expected to influence teacher enthu- siasm on its own (Cheng and Xie  2018). Similarly, although components such as AI- TCK and AI- TPK are important for instructional planning, teachers' proficiency in these areas may not necessarily lead to increased emotional motivation or excitement. Since these types of knowledge are primarily tech- nical and application- oriented, their capacity to trigger emo- tional responses may be limited (Lan et al. 2025; Lorenz and Romeike 2023). Moreover, although the AI- TPACK component represents the integration of all domains, teachers may strug- gle to operationalise this conceptual unity in their daily prac- tice. This may help explain why this component shows a weak association with emotional engagement (Mishra et  al.  2023). These findings suggest that teacher enthusiasm is more closely linked to pedagogical knowledge directly related to instruction and to technology knowledge grounded in personal experience. Therefore, future research could benefit from focusing on how teachers perceive and experience these knowledge components, as this may enhance understanding of the findings.

**5.4 \| Gender- Based Differences in AI- TPACK and Pedagogical Variables**

The results of the MGA revealed significant gender- based differences in how teachers' AI- TPACK components and ped- agogical competencies predict teacher enthusiasm. This find- ing suggests that both cognitive and affective outcomes are structured through different patterns depending on gender. PK significantly predicted teacher enthusiasm only in the female teacher group, while AI- TK did so only in the male teacher group. This suggests that professional commitment and motivation are more strongly associated with pedagogi- cal values in female teachers, and with technical competence in male teachers. Indeed, previous studies have also indicated that female teachers tend to develop a stronger emotional attachment to pedagogical activities, which contributes to their professional enthusiasm (Keller et  al.  2016; Tondeur et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2024; Yue et al. [2024)](#appendix). When inter- preted within the framework of Bandura's  ([1986)](#such-an-approach-may-promote-equitable-participation-of-both-acknowledgements-female-and-male-teachers-in-ai--integrated-instructional-prac-) SCT, this divergence aligns with the proposition that teachers' interac- tions with their self- efficacy beliefs and environmental sup- port structures may differ based on individual characteristics. It appears that female teachers tend to construct their ped- agogical competencies more meaningfully through social in- teractions and collaboration, whereas male teachers reinforce their self- efficacy in technical knowledge primarily through individual experiences. These results are also consistent with pedagogical adaptations of the TAM. Male teachers' willing- ness to integrate AI technologies into instructional processes appears to be largely influenced by perceived ease of use and technological competence (Runge et al. 2025; Teo 2011).

It was observed that the AI- TCK and AI- TPACK compo- nents did not significantly predict teacher enthusiasm. This result indicates that integrated and content- focused types of knowledge tend to establish indirect relationships with af- fective outcomes. Feldman- Maggor et  al.  (2025) emphasise that such types of knowledge structures are more closely re- lated to teachers' cognitive processes and may have limited 

_European Journal of Education,_ 2025

associations with affective variables. In this context, for AI- TPACK components to influence motivation, they may need to be well understood and made functional within the pedagog- ical context by teachers. Knowledge types such as CK, PCK, AI- TCK, and AI- TPK did not significantly predict teacher en- thusiasm in either gender group. These constructs reflect the cognitive knowledge base possessed by teachers, but do not directly impact affective outcomes. Hava and Babayiğit (2025) highlight that technical competence alone is insufficient to enhance instructional motivation, and that the pedagogical contextualisation of competencies is crucial in generating in- structional impact.

Teacher collaboration emerged as a significant predictor of the development of both pedagogical and technological knowl- edge types across both gender groups. Collaboration supports teachers' knowledge sharing, joint planning, and professional learning processes, positively influencing the development of both traditional and AI- based knowledge types. In particular, teacher collaboration demonstrated significant associations with PK, CK, PCK, AI- TCK, AI- TPK, and AI- TPACK com- ponents. These findings support previous studies emphasis- ing that teacher interaction serves as a critical resource for the development of digital pedagogical competencies (Chai et al. 2010; Koh et al. 2014). This suggests that collaboration contributes more to knowledge generation while remaining limited in its direct impact on affective outcomes. However, contextual variables such as AI usage frequency, AI experi- ence, and digital competence did not significantly predict teacher enthusiasm, regardless of gender. This finding indi- cates that teacher enthusiasm is related not merely to expo- sure to technology, but to how that technology is interpreted within the instructional process. Cheng and Xie (2018) em- phasise that the effective use of technological tools will have limited impact on affective outcomes unless integrated with pedagogical understanding. The findings highlight the impor- tance of gender- sensitive intervention programmes in teacher education processes. Therefore, addressing the AI- TPACK framework in a manner that is sensitive to individual differ- ences will play a pivotal role in the success of technological transformation processes.

**5.5 \| Limitations and Directions for Future Research**

This study examined the interactions among teachers' indi- vidual and professional characteristics, levels of collaboration, AI- TPACK components, and teacher enthusiasm using a mul- tilevel model, offering meaningful theoretical and practical contributions. However, the findings should be interpreted in light of certain limitations. The sample of the study was limited to teachers working in Türkiye. This may lead to lim- itations in external validity due to cultural, technological, and institutional contextual differences. In particular, factors such as educational policies, levels of digital infrastructure, and the institutional acceptance of AI technologies may vary across countries. Therefore, testing similar structural models in dif- ferent countries is important for evaluating cross- cultural validity. The design of the study is limited to cross- sectional 

data. This limits the ability to make causal inferences about the relationships among variables. Longitudinal research de- signs are needed to analyse how AI- TPACK competencies and teacher enthusiasm evolve over time, the long- term effects of teacher collaboration, and the developmental trajectory of technology acceptance. The data collection tools are based on self- report measures. This may lead participants to overesti- mate their competence or willingness, particularly in areas such as AI usage and pedagogical proficiency. Therefore, future studies are encouraged to adopt mixed- methods ap- proaches supported by qualitative data sources (e.g., inter- views, classroom observations, journals). Fourth, although the AI- TPACK scale used in this study measures teachers' multidimensional competencies related to AI- Ed, it does not include micro- level details on how specific AI components are translated into pedagogical contexts. At this point, qualitative content analyses and case studies that examine how GenAI tools (e.g., ChatGPT, DALL·E, Copilot) are positioned within classroom scenarios could be developed. The low _R_2 values obtained for certain constructs in the model (e.g., AI- TPACK, teacher collaboration) suggest that other variables outside the model may also influence these constructs. In particular, in- vestigating the impact of organisational and psychosocial fac- tors—such as teachers' beliefs, institutional support systems, school leadership, and levels of digital autonomy—on AI- based pedagogical practices could provide meaningful direc- tions for future research. It is important for future studies to contextualise teacher education processes not only at the indi- vidual level but also by employing ecosystem- focused, multi- level models that promote more inclusive and comprehensive understandings. To support the development of AI- TPACK competencies, the effects of innovative approaches—such as design- based research, professional learning communities, and feedback systems based on learning analytics—should also be systematically tested.

In this study, data were collected through self- report- based scales. This raises the possibility that response biases—particularly so- cial desirability bias—may pose limitations on the validity of the measurements. In particular, participants' perception- based responses may reflect a certain degree of subjectivity when as- sessing constructs with strong affective and cognitive compo- nents—such as teacher enthusiasm, AI- TPACK competencies, and professional collaboration. To mitigate the potential effects of this limitation and enhance the validity of future findings, it is recommended that upcoming studies employ triangulation strat- egies—such as qualitative observations, structured interviews, or the integration of multiple data sources.

This study provides a valuable cross- sectional perspective on the relationships among AI- TPACK components, teacher collabora- tion, and enthusiasm; however, its capacity to explore how these constructs evolve over time remains limited. Future longitudi- nal studies could investigate the developmental trajectory of AI- TPACK competencies and the long- term effects of practices such as professional collaboration or AI- focused training on teacher enthusiasm. Research questions may aim to reveal the temporal sequence of changes in pedagogical competencies and the medi- ating role of time in the interaction among cognitive, affective, and contextual variables.
